parts.text:
3
Two forces of equal magnitude are represented by two coplanar vectors. One is directed towards
the east and the other is directed towards the north.
What is the direction of a single force that will balance these two forces?
A
towards the north-east
B
towards the north-west
C
towards the south-east
D
towards the south-west

hints: Notice the two given forces point east and north with equal magnitude, so sketch them tail-to-tail pointing to the right and up.
Recall that the resultant of east plus north points midway between them into the north-east quadrant.
Recall that to balance forces the single force must give zero vector sum, so it must point exactly opposite to that resultant.
walkthrough: Draw the two equal forces from one point: one arrow to the east and one arrow to the north at $90^{\circ}$ to each other.
Add them by the parallelogram or triangle rule. Because the magnitudes are equal, the diagonal lies exactly midway between east and north.
That resultant therefore points towards the north-east.
For balance, the vector sum of all three forces must be zero, so the third force must be equal in magnitude and opposite in direction to this resultant.
Opposite to north-east is south-west. This is option D.

A.explanation: This is the direction of the resultant of the east and north forces, not the opposite force needed to cancel it.

B.explanation: A north-west force has a west component which cannot cancel an eastward force.

C.explanation: A south-east force has an east component which would add to the eastward force instead of cancelling it.

D.explanation: South-west is opposite to north-east, so its south component cancels north and its west component cancels east for zero resultant.
